item.title: Building an Automated Backup Pipeline for Keycloak Database and Step-by-Step Recovery Verification Methodologies
item.description:
As infrastructure scaling and multi-tenant integration progress, when Keycloak serves as the Single Sign-On (SSO) gateway for Kubernetes API OpenID Connect (OIDC) authentication and major CI/CD tools such as ArgoCD and Jenkins, its backend database becomes a Single Point of Failure (SPOF) for the entire system. Operations relying on a single PostgreSQL Pod or Local PersistentVolume carry the risk that a node hardware failure or logical data corruption will immediately halt all downstream engineering workflows.

Because constructing an active-active multi-master DB introduces high architectural complexity, establishing an automated backup combining primary evacuation to an NFS PVC with secondary replication to S3-compatible storage, alongside a phased disaster recovery rehearsal (DR Rehearsal) to empirically verify Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO), is essential as a baseline operational safety standard.

Architecture Configuration and Prerequisites

The target standard infrastructure configuration and access requirements are as follows:

  • Identity Management: Keycloak v26.x (deployed via Keycloak Operator, spec.instances: 1)
  • Database Engine: PostgreSQL 15 (single-replica StatefulSet, internal Service postgres-db:5432)
  • Storage Allocation: PersistentVolume bound to node-local disk /data

Critical Access Prerequisites (Avoiding OIDC Dependency)

Before executing disaster recovery rehearsals or troubleshooting, ensure cluster administrator privileges using a direct X.509 certificate-based kubeconfig (admin.conf) that does not rely on Keycloak OIDC tokens. If kubectl authentication relies on OIDC during a Keycloak database disconnection or rebuild, all API access will be blocked, resulting in a deadlock where recovery operations themselves become impossible.

Implementation of a Two-Tier Storage Backup Pipeline

Backup data must be completely isolated from the production database compute and storage domains.

  • Tier-1 (Local Staging): Shared Network File System (NFS PVC). Avoids external network transfer bottlenecks and achieves a fast RTO.
  • Tier-2 (Offsite Disaster Recovery): S3-compatible object storage. Protects data against hypervisor outages or physical destruction of local disks.

The following Kubernetes CronJob manifest automates binary format (-Fc) extraction using pg_dump, SHA-256 checksum verification, and transfer to S3 with integrity verification using rclone.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
 name: keycloak-db-backup
 namespace: keycloak
spec:
 schedule: "0 2 * * *"
 timeZone: "Asia/Tokyo"
 concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
 jobTemplate:
 spec:
 backoffLimit: 1
 template:
 spec:
 restartPolicy: Never
 initContainers:
 - name: pg-dump
 image: postgres:15
 env:
 - name: PGHOST
 value: postgres-db
 - name: PGDATABASE
 value: keycloak
 - name: PGUSER
 valueFrom:
 secretKeyRef:
 name: keycloak-db-secret
 key: username
 - name: PGPASSWORD
 valueFrom:
 secretKeyRef:
 name: keycloak-db-secret
 key: password
 command: ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
 args:
 - |
 set -euo pipefail
 N="keycloak-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).dump"
 cd /backup
 
 # Execute binary dump in custom format
 pg_dump -Fc -f "$N"
 
 # Verify dump file header structure and readability
 pg_restore -l "$N" > /dev/null
 
 # Generate SHA256 hash
 sha256sum "$N" > "$N.sha256"
 
 # Update pointer to latest file
 echo "$N" > .latest
 
 # Automatically delete local backups older than 7 days
 find /backup -name 'keycloak-*.dump*' -mtime +7 -delete
 volumeMounts:
 - name: backup
 mountPath: /backup
 containers:
 - name: upload
 image: rclone/rclone:1.68
 env:
 - name: RCLONE_CONFIG_BK_TYPE
 value: s3
 - name: RCLONE_CONFIG_BK_PROVIDER
 value: Other
 - name: RCLONE_CONFIG_BK_ENDPOINT
 value: "http://s3-storage.internal:9000"
 - name: RCLONE_CONFIG_BK_ACCESS_KEY_ID
 valueFrom:
 secretKeyRef:
 name: keycloak-db-s3
 key: ACCESS_KEY_ID
 - name: RCLONE_CONFIG_BK_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
 valueFrom:
 secretKeyRef:
 name: keycloak-db-s3
 key: ACCESS_SECRET_KEY
 - name: DEST
 value: "bk:keycloak-db-backup/pgdump"
 command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
 args:
 - |
 set -eu
 N=$(cat /backup/.latest)
 
 # Transfer assets to S3 storage
 rclone copyto "/backup/$N" "$DEST/$N"
 rclone copyto "/backup/$N.sha256" "$DEST/$N.sha256"
 
 # Remote verification: Recalculate hash from S3 stream to verify integrity
 L=$(awk '{print $1}' "/backup/$N.sha256")
 R=$(rclone cat "$DEST/$N" | sha256sum | awk '{print $1}')
 
 if [ "$L" != "$R" ]; then
 echo "CRITICAL: Remote checksum mismatch for: $N"
 exit 1
 fi
 
 echo "Uploaded and verified: $N"
 
 # Delete remote backups older than 30 days
 rclone delete "$DEST" --min-age 30d --include 'keycloak-*.dump*'
 volumeMounts:
 - name: backup
 mountPath: /backup
 readOnly: true
 volumes:
 - name: backup
 persistentVolumeClaim:
 claimName: keycloak-db-backup

Phased Recovery Rehearsals (Disaster Recovery Rehearsal)

Recovery capabilities are verified in three phases according to the level of risk to the production environment.

Level 1: Schema and Record Integrity Verification in a Non-Destructive Isolated Pod

Verify restore success and record counts by launching a temporary Pod without impacting production traffic or the running PostgreSQL instance.

# Deploy temporary verification Pod and wait
kubectl apply -f - <<eof "$(basename="" "$f"="" "$q"="" #="" $f).sha256"="" &&="" '="" -="" --="" --exit-on-error="" --for="condition=Ready" --no-owner="" --timeout="120s" -1)="" -c="" -d="" -n="" -t="" -u="" 2;="" \="" against="" and="" apiversion:="" backup="" baseline="" bash="" cd="" check="" claimname:="" compare="" containers:="" count="" do="" done="" env:="" eof="" exec="" execute="" f="$(ls" head="" image:="" integrity="" keycloak="" keycloak-*.dump="" keycloak-db-backup="" keycloak;="" kind:="" kubectl="" metadata:="" mountpath:="" name:="" namespace:="" never="" persistentvolumeclaim:="" pg_isready="" pg_restore="" pod="" postgres="" postgres:15="" postgres_db="" postgres_password="" postgres_user="" pre-acquired="" psql="" q="SELECT 'realm', count(*) FROM realm UNION ALL SELECT 'client', count(*) FROM client UNION ALL SELECT 'user_entity', count(*) FROM user_entity;" readonly:="" record="" restartpolicy:="" restore="" restore-test="" sha256sum="" sleep="" spec:="" the="" true="" until="" v1="" value:="" verify="" volumemounts:="" volumes:="" wait="" |=""> count-restore.txt
diff -u count-before.txt count-restore.txt && echo "CHECK_SUCCESS: Record counts match baseline."

# Clean up resources
kubectl delete pod restore-test -n keycloak

Level 2: In-Place Database Failure Restoration and RTO Measurement

Rebuild the database after stopping Keycloak, assuming logical data corruption.

  1. Stopping Keycloak Pods (Preventing Race Conditions):

    kubectl patch keycloak keycloak -n keycloak --type merge -p '{"spec":{"instances":0}}'

  2. Database Re-creation and Restore:

    kubectl exec -n keycloak postgresql-db-0 -- psql -U keycloak -d postgres -c 'DROP DATABASE keycloak;'
kubectl exec -n keycloak postgresql-db-0 -- psql -U keycloak -d postgres -c 'CREATE DATABASE keycloak OWNER keycloak;'

kubectl exec -n keycloak postgresql-db-0 -- bash -c '
 set -euo pipefail
 cd /backup
 F=$(ls -t keycloak-*.dump | head -1)
 sha256sum -c "$F.sha256"
 pg_restore -U keycloak -d keycloak --no-owner --exit-on-error "$F"

 # クラスタリングキャッシュ情報の初期化
 psql -U keycloak -d keycloak -c "TRUNCATE jgroups_ping;" || true
'

  3. Keycloak Restart and Health Checks:

    kubectl patch keycloak keycloak -n keycloak --type merge -p '{"spec":{"instances":1}}'
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready keycloak/keycloak -n keycloak --timeout=600s

Level 3: DR Recovery from Complete Loss of Node and Local Storage

This recovery flow is for cases where the local PV (/data) is physically lost due to a node failure. Re-define the PVC on a different node and pull data directly back from S3 to restore.

# Back up the target StatefulSet definition and delete it
kubectl patch keycloak keycloak -n keycloak --type merge -p '{"spec":{"instances":0}}'
kubectl get sts postgresql-db -n keycloak -o yaml > sts-backup.yaml
kubectl delete sts postgresql-db -n keycloak

# Recreate the StatefulSet by reallocating to PV/PVC on the new node
# (Apply after editing volumeClaimTemplates in sts-backup.yaml)
kubectl apply -f sts-backup.yaml

# Pull dump directly from S3 and restore
kubectl exec -n keycloak postgresql-db-0 -- bash -c '
 rclone copyto bk:keycloak-db-backup/pgdump/latest.dump /backup/latest.dump
 pg_restore -U keycloak -d keycloak --no-owner /backup/latest.dump
'

Operational Logs

Output logs from restore verification and comparison protocols executed on an actual system.

$ kubectl get keycloak,sts,pod,svc,pvc -n keycloak -o wide
NAME READY CLIENTS PROVIDER AGE
keycloak.k8s.keycloak.org/keycloak 1/1 1 db 45d

NAME READY AGE CONTAINERS IMAGES
statefulset.apps/postgresql-db 1/1 45d postgres postgres:15

NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE IP NODE
pod/postgresql-db-0 1/1 Running 0 45d 10.244.3.12 infra-node-02

$ kubectl exec -n keycloak restore-test -- bash -c 'cd /backup && sha256sum -c keycloak-20261121-020000.dump.sha256'
keycloak-20261121-020000.dump: OK

$ kubectl exec -n keycloak restore-test -- bash -c 'pg_restore -U keycloak -d keycloak --no-owner --exit-on-error keycloak-20261121-020000.dump'
pg_restore: processing item 4201 TABLE DATA realm
pg_restore: processing item 4205 TABLE DATA client
pg_restore: processing item 4210 TABLE DATA user_entity
pg_restore: restore completed successfully without errors

$ diff -u count-before.txt count-restore.txt
--- count-before.txt 2026-11-21 01:55:00.000000000 +0900
+++ count-restore.txt 2026-11-21 02:15:30.000000000 +0900
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
- realm | 3
- client | 42
- user_entity | 1250
+ realm | 3
+ client | 42
+ user_entity | 1250
CHECK_SUCCESS: Record counts match baseline.

Troubleshooting

1. Inability to Execute kubectl Operations Due to OIDC Authentication Token Dependency

  • Symptom: Keycloak stops following the database shutdown, and executing kubectl fails with Error: Unauthorized or Token Renewal errors, rejecting recovery Pod deployment operations.
  • Cause: The client’s kubeconfig is configured with Keycloak OIDC as the authentication provider.
  • Mitigation: During DR procedures, switch the context to X.509 client certificate authentication (admin.conf) issued directly by the Kubernetes Control Plane API server before executing operations.

2. jgroups_ping Cluster Lockout During Keycloak Startup After Restore

  • Symptom: After database restoration, starting Keycloak Pods results in repeated log outputs of JGRP00006: failed sending message, failing to transition to Ready state.
  • Cause: IP addresses or node identifiers from the old environment remain in the DB’s jgroups_ping table, causing a deadlock during cluster node discovery with new Pods.
  • Mitigation: Immediately after DB restore and prior to Keycloak startup, execute TRUNCATE TABLE jgroups_ping; to initialize the discovery table.

3. Version Mismatch Error Between pg_dump and pg_restore

  • Symptom: During restore execution, pg_restore: error: unsupported version (1.15) in file header occurs and processing halts.
  • Cause: A version discrepancy exists between the PostgreSQL image tag of the container that performed the backup and the target restore Pod (e.g., PostgreSQL 14 vs 15).
  • Mitigation: Pin the image tags of both the backup Job and verification Pod to the same major version (postgres:15).

4. Hash Verification Failure Due to Transient Network Interruptions During S3 Transfer

  • Symptom: The CronJob’s upload container outputs CRITICAL: Remote checksum mismatch and transitions to a Failed state.
  • Cause: An incomplete multipart upload occurred during the upload of a large dump file, resulting in missing data length on S3.
  • Mitigation: Apply retries by adding the --checksum flag during rclone copyto execution, and allow the Job to automatically retry upon transfer errors based on backoffLimit.

Operational Notes

  1. Storage Domain Isolation Principle: Saving backup files to the same physical disk as the production PostgreSQL database is invalid for DR design. Ensure redundancy across a separate network NFS and S3-compatible storage.
  2. JGroups Cache Initialization: During database recovery, substantial timeouts will occur in Keycloak cluster node discovery unless the jgroups_ping table is explicitly purged.
  3. Handling Offline Sessions: Tokens or active sessions issued between the time of backup creation and restoration will be lost. Establish deletion policies for offline_user_session in advance according to business requirements.
  4. Standardization of Periodic Rehearsals: In addition to automating backup configurations, establishing operational procedures to perform Level 1 and Level 2 recovery rehearsals quarterly and recording measured RTO values in audit logs is recommended.

item.title: Implementation of Performance Improvement and Automation for NAS-Google Drive Synchronization Using rclone
item.description:
In the synchronization operation between NAS and Google Drive (Google Workspace Shared Drive), a serious performance bottleneck was identified from operational data after the initial setup. This article describes the process of introducing a dedicated API key and optimizing the synchronization cycle to improve transfer speeds and eliminate synchronization delays.

1. Current Status Analysis and Issue Identification

As a result of conducting an operational test for approximately two weeks in an environment synchronizing 1.1 TB of ipTIME NAS data to Google Drive, the following two constraints were identified.

Stagnant Transfer Speeds: Despite being in a gigabit network environment, the speed during rclone copy execution hovered around 1 MB/s to 3 MB/s. Especially in directories containing tens of thousands of small files, it took a significant amount of time to complete synchronization.

Business Impact due to Sync Delays: With the initially configured schedule of “once a day (2:00 AM),” documents created in the morning were not reflected in the cloud until the following day, leading to situations where users requiring immediacy manually transferred files.

2. Technical Root Cause: Shared API Quota Limits

In rclone’s default configuration, the “Global Default OAuth Client ID” shared by users worldwide is used. Google APIs have per-second and per-day request limits (quotas) set for each client ID, and using a shared ID easily leads to reaching these limits due to the influence of other users.

When limits are reached, Google returns errors such as API rate exceeded or userRateLimitExceeded, and rclone enters a backoff (waiting) state. This is the direct cause of the extreme drop in effective throughput. To resolve this issue, it is necessary to issue an organization-specific OAuth client ID/secret in the Google Cloud Console to secure a dedicated quota.

3. Issuing and Configuring a Dedicated API Key

3.1 Configuration in Google Cloud Console

Project Creation: Create a new project (e.g., rclone-sync-project) in the Google Cloud Console (https://console.cloud.google.com).

Enabling the API: Search for and enable “Google Drive API” from “APIs & Services > Library”.

OAuth Consent Screen Configuration: Set the user type to “Internal” on the “OAuth consent screen”. This restricts usage to users within the Google Workspace domain and avoids token expiration issues.

Creating Credentials: Select “Credentials > Create Credentials > OAuth client ID”. Specify “Desktop app” as the application type.

Saving the ID and Secret: Record the generated “Client ID” and “Client Secret” in a secure location.

3.2 Updating rclone Configuration

Apply the new credentials to the existing remote configuration.

[gdrive]
type = drive
client_id = your_own_client_id.apps.googleusercontent.com
client_secret = your_own_client_secret
scope = drive

4. Optimization of Synchronization Automation (2-Hour Cycle)

Considering the balance between data freshness and system load, the synchronization frequency is set to a 2-hour cycle. The bisync command, which maintains bidirectional consistency, is adopted for synchronization.

4.1 Creating the Synchronization Batch File

Configure the following script as C:\rclone\sync.bat. By applying the dedicated API key, throttling is less likely to occur even if –transfers (number of concurrent transfers) is increased to 8.

@echo off
rclone bisync C:\nas_data gdrive:shared_drive --transfers 8 --log-file C:\rclone\rclone.log --verbose

4.2 Windows Task Scheduler Configuration

General: Select “Run whether user is logged on or not” and “Run with highest privileges”.

Triggers: Set to run daily, repeat task every “2 hours”, for a duration of “1 day”.

Actions: Specify C:\rclone\sync.bat and enter C:\rclone in “Start in (optional)”.

Settings: Set “If the task is already running, then the following rule applies” to “Do not start a new instance” to prevent overlapping processes.

5. Post-Implementation Performance Comparison

Metric Phase 1 (Default API + Once a Day) Phase 2 (Dedicated API + 2-Hour Cycle)
Average Transfer Speed 1–3 MB/s 15–30 MB/s
Sync Delay (Max) 24 hours 2 hours
Throttling Occurrence Frequent Almost resolved
System Load Concentrated at midnight (high burst) Distributed execution (low load)

Operational Notes

Token Expiration: If the OAuth consent screen is in the “External” and “Testing” state, the token will expire in 7 days. Be sure to verify that it is in the “Internal” or “In production” state.

Log Management: Log output via –log-file is mandatory. It serves as the sole diagnostic means when synchronization errors or conflicts occur.

bisync Characteristics: Since bisync checks path consistency during the initial run, it takes time only for the first execution in large directories. Once in stable operation, it scans only the changed deltas, completing in a few minutes.
